headline: Monthly GDP Contracts 0.6% as Manufacturing Falls 4.6% YoY, BoC Holds at 2.25%
executive_summary:
Statistics Canada's monthly real GDP by industry print recorded a -0.6%5 month-over-month contraction, with manufacturing GDP down 1.4% month-over-month and -4.6% year-over-year and management of companies and enterprises (NAICS 55) down 4.1% month-over-month and -21.9% year-over-year, the deepest annual contraction among 20 tracked industries.5 Construction GDP rose 1.1% month-over-month and 2.8% year-over-year, partially offsetting the broader monthly decline. The project database tracks 52 manufacturing projects ($67.4B) and 1,687 infrastructure projects ($179.0B) in the affected NAICS sectors.

The Bank of Canada overnight rate held at 2.25%1 following the March 5, 2026 decision, the seventh consecutive hold at this level. The prime rate sits at 6.09%2 and the 2-year Government of Canada yield at 2.95%, approximately 70 basis points above the policy rate.2 The next BoC decision is scheduled for April 16, 2026. Headline CPI registered +1.8%3 year-over-year in March, within the central bank's 1-3% target band, with a 6.5 percentage-point provincial dispersion ranging from PE +5.4% to ON -1.1% and SK -0.7%.3

The Labour Force Survey recorded national unemployment at 6.7%4 in March 2026, with a 4.5 percentage-point provincial spread between Saskatchewan at 5.0% (lowest) and Newfoundland and Labrador at 9.5% (highest).4 Construction employment stood at 1,998,800, manufacturing employment at 249,600, and mining and oil and gas extraction employment at 350,300.9 The participation rate carried at 64.9% from the February observation, 71 days old at the time of refresh.4

Brent crude settled at US$96.52/bbl10 on April 9, 2026, down 11.47% week-over-week and up 47.40% year-over-year. The WTI Yahoo scrape was flagged as unreliable this week and is not cited. Statistics Canada's Non-residential Capital and Repair Expenditures release places 2026 capital expenditure intentions at $401.2B7, of which $274.0B is construction and $127.2B machinery and equipment.7 The pipeline tracks 7,344 active projects worth $1,366.6B across 13 provinces and territories. The Bank of Canada April 16 rate decision and the federal budget release scheduled on or about April 15 follow next week, alongside the March CPI release on April 17.

national.analysis:
Canada's monthly real GDP by industry contracted -0.6%5 in the latest Statistics Canada print, reversing the prior month's +0.1% reading. Manufacturing GDP (NAICS 31-33) fell 1.4% month-over-month and 4.6% year-over-year, the steepest goods-producing decline in the release. Management of companies and enterprises (NAICS 55) recorded the deepest annual contraction in the table at -21.9% year-over-year and -4.1% month-over-month.5 Construction (NAICS 23) rose 1.1% month-over-month and 2.8% year-over-year, while mining, quarrying and oil and gas extraction (NAICS 21) gained 1.2% month-over-month against a -0.1% annual base.5 Wholesale trade (NAICS 41) declined 1.2% month-over-month and 1.7% year-over-year; transportation and warehousing (NAICS 48-49) fell 0.7% month-over-month against a +1.6% annual base.5

The Labour Force Survey recorded unemployment at 6.7%4 in March 2026, unchanged from the prior print. Employment fell 84,000 in February after gaining 76,000 in January, with full-time employment down 108,000 and part-time employment up 24,000.4 Private sector employment fell 73,000 and public sector employment fell 11,000.4 Industry-level employment from Table 14-10-0022 placed construction employment at 1,998,800, manufacturing at 249,600, and mining and oil and gas extraction at 350,300.9 Wage growth ran at +3.9% year-over-year per Survey of Employment, Payrolls and Hours data.21 The participation rate carried at 64.9%, observed February 1, 2026 and 71 days old at the time of this refresh.4

Headline CPI rose 1.8%3 year-over-year in March 2026, down 0.5 percentage points from the prior print. Provincial CPI dispersion spans 6.5 percentage points: PE +5.4%, AB +3.4%, MB +3.1%, NL +1.8%, NS +1.5%, NB +1.2%, BC +1.0%, QC +0.6%, SK -0.7%, and ON -1.1%.3 Core CPI median ran at 2.3%, shelter CPI at +1.5%, food CPI at 5.3%, and energy CPI at -14.2%.3 Statistics Canada's January merchandise trade report placed the trade deficit at $3.6B, widened from $1.3B, with exports down 4.7% to $62.5B and imports down 1.1% to $66.1B; motor vehicle exports fell 21.2%. January retail sales rose 1.1% to $70.7B, with motor vehicle dealers up 2.0% and core retail (ex gasoline and motor vehicles) up 0.9%; the advance February estimate was +0.9%.

CMHC housing starts ran at 250,900 SAAR6, up 4.5% from the prior print of 240,148. Building permits totalled $13.3B22 in January, up 4.8%, of which residential permits were $25.9B (annualized basis) and non-residential $10.3B.22 Statistics Canada's Non-residential Capital and Repair Expenditures release places 2026 capital expenditure intentions at $401.2B7, of which $274.0B is construction and $127.2B machinery and equipment.7 The pipeline tracks 211 residential projects ($44.4B), 1,687 infrastructure projects ($179.0B), and a total of 7,344 active projects worth $1,366.6B.

consumer_pulse:
Consumer-facing data points centred on the 1.8%3 headline CPI and the 6.5 percentage-point provincial inflation spread between PE at +5.4% and ON at -1.1%.3 Shelter CPI ran at +1.5%, food CPI at +5.3%, and core CPI median at 2.3%, while energy CPI fell 14.2% year-over-year.3 Average home price stood at $663,828 per CREA data, with January retail sales of $70.7B (+1.1% month-over-month) and an advance February estimate of +0.9% month-over-month. Motor vehicle dealers led January retail with a +2.0% gain, and core retail (ex gasoline and motor vehicles) rose 0.9%.

The Conference Board of Canada consumer confidence index registered 47.50 in February, down 1.80 points from 49.30 in January. The Bloomberg-Nanos index recorded a three-week slide into late March. The Labour Force Survey placed national unemployment at 6.7%4, with the provincial spread running from SK 5.0% to NL 9.5%.4 February employment fell 84,000, with full-time employment down 108,000, part-time employment up 24,000, private sector employment down 73,000, and public sector employment down 11,000.4 Wage growth ran at +3.9% year-over-year per the Survey of Employment, Payrolls and Hours, 2.1 percentage points above headline CPI.21 Word-cloud topics captured this week included PE inflation above 5%, ON CPI -1.1%, BoC overnight rate at 2.25%, prime rate 6.09%, housing affordability, NL unemployment 9.5%, manufacturing GDP -4.6% YoY, capex intentions of $401.2B, and uranium proxies up 130% year-over-year.

global.analysis:
The US Federal Reserve federal funds rate stood at 3.64%25 in the February 2026 print, 139 basis points above the Bank of Canada overnight rate of 2.25%.1 US unemployment ran at 4.4%24 in February, while the US CPI index registered 327.46 for the same period.24 US real GDP carried at $24,066B for Q3 2025; the BEA Q4 2025 release was pending at the time of refresh.23 CAD/USD settled at 0.723513 on April 9, 2026, up 0.70% on the week and +2.03% year-over-year. The 139-basis-point rate differential between the Federal Reserve and the Bank of Canada is one factor in the cross-border yield gap captured in this week's data.

US benchmark equities closed sharply higher on April 9, 2026: the S&P 500 at 6,824.66, up 3.68% on the day and +25.06% year-over-year; the Dow Jones Industrial Average at 48,185.80, up 3.61% on the day and +18.66% year-over-year; and the NASDAQ Composite at 22,822.42, up 4.31% on the day and +33.27% year-over-year.12 The S&P/TSX Composite tracked at +41.10% year-over-year, above all three US benchmarks on a 12-month basis.11 Statistics Canada's January merchandise trade release recorded total Canadian exports of $62.5B against imports of $66.1B, with motor vehicle exports down 21.2% month-over-month — a category dominated by the Canada-US cross-border supply chain.

global.analysis:
USD/CNY stood at 6.82872 on April 8, 2026, down 1.0% month-over-month and 7.0% year-over-year, indicating yuan appreciation against the US dollar over the trailing 12 months. China-linked commodity benchmarks recorded mixed prints on the week. Iron ore settled at $107.83/t19, up 0.30% week-over-week and +8.64% year-over-year. Copper closed at US$5.75/lb16, up 3.32% on the week and +37.65% year-over-year. Aluminum registered $3,369.50/t, down 1.22% on the week and up 55.55% year-over-year.

The project database tracks 367 mining projects ($159.5B) with exposure to China commodity demand across iron ore, copper, aluminum and potash, plus 61 oil and gas projects ($100.2B). Nutrien (the potash proxy) closed at $72.7818, down 3.56% on the week and up 50.34% year-over-year. The Sprott Physical Uranium Trust proxy registered $50.93/share17, up 4.15% on the week and +130.24% year-over-year, on a 52-week range of $21.59 to $61.81. Canadian commodity mining sector GDP (NAICS 21) rose 1.2% month-over-month against a -0.1% year-over-year base in the latest StatCan industry print.5

global.analysis:
Eurozone HICP ran at +1.9%27 year-over-year in the December 2025 print, the latest captured in the data set. The European Central Bank deposit rate stood at 2.75%26 in the February 2025 capture, flagged in the dossier as stale relative to subsequent ECB decisions. The DAX closed at 24,080.6329 on April 8, 2026, up 3.36% on the day, +2.87% month-over-month, and +18.74% year-over-year.29 EUR/USD traded at 1.1696 on April 9, up 1.34% on the week, +0.68% month-over-month, and +6.79% year-over-year.

The euro's +6.79% 12-month appreciation against the US dollar carries implications for cross-border pricing of Canadian exports to the European Union. The DAX +18.74% 12-month gain tracks below the S&P/TSX Composite's +41.10% year-over-year advance and the S&P 500's +25.06%. Statistics Canada's January merchandise trade release recorded total Canadian exports of $62.5B against imports of $66.1B, generating a $3.6B trade deficit, with exports down 4.7% month-over-month and imports down 1.1%. Eurozone HICP at +1.9% year-over-year tracks slightly above the Canadian headline CPI print of +1.8% for March 2026.3

global.analysis:
The FTSE 100 closed at 10,608.9028 on April 8, 2026, up 2.36% on the day, +3.51% month-over-month, and +34.11% year-over-year, the second-largest 12-month equity gain among the captured benchmarks after the Nikkei 225 at +70.57%.30 GBP/USD traded at 1.3432 on April 9, 2026, up 1.5% on the week, +0.1% month-over-month, and +4.7% year-over-year. The GBP/USD value was carried from the prior briefing because the timeseries.json file did not include an fx_gbpusd entry this week.

The Bank of England policy rate and UK CPI series were not present in the on-disk data set this week. The FTSE 100 +34.11% 12-month gain tracks below the S&P/TSX Composite's +41.10% year-over-year advance and above the S&P 500's +25.06% over the same period. The pound's +4.7% 12-month advance against the US dollar carries implications for cross-border pricing of Canadian exports to the United Kingdom. Brent crude — the dominant North Sea benchmark — settled at US$96.52/bbl10 on April 9, 2026, down 11.47% week-over-week and up 47.40% year-over-year, on a 52-week range of $58.92 to $118.35 and a one-year average of $69.87. The pipeline tracks 61 oil and gas projects ($100.2B).
